title: Pages & Layouts
summary: In the App Router, a **`page.tsx`** makes a route segment publicly accessible, while a **`layout.tsx`** wraps that page (and everything below it) in shared UI that **persists across navigation** — and a special **root layout** defines the `<html>`/`<body>` shell for the whole app.

subtopics.title: page.tsx — what makes a route public
subtopics.explanation: A folder under `app/` only becomes a navigable URL when it contains a `page.tsx` (or `page.js`). The component default-exported from that file is the unique UI rendered for that route. Folders without a `page.tsx` are just structure — they organize routes but aren't reachable themselves.

subtopics.title: layout.tsx — shared UI that persists
subtopics.explanation: A `layout.tsx` wraps its segment's `page.tsx` and all nested segments. It MUST accept a `children` prop and render it. The key property: when you navigate between routes that share a layout, the layout does NOT re-render or unmount — only the changing `page` content swaps. That preserves state (scroll, form input, players) and avoids re-fetching layout data.

subtopics.title: The root layout (required)
subtopics.explanation: Every App Router app needs exactly one root layout at `app/layout.tsx`. It's the only layout that can (and must) render the `<html>` and `<body>` tags, since it replaces the document shell. It also can't be removed and applies to every route. This is where you put global providers, fonts, and the top-level metadata.

subtopics.title: Nested layouts
subtopics.explanation: Layouts nest automatically by folder depth. A request to `/dashboard/settings` renders root layout → dashboard layout → settings layout → settings page, each wrapping the next. This lets you compose UI: a global header in the root, a section sidebar in the dashboard layout, and so on, without repeating markup.

subtopics.title: Templates vs layouts
subtopics.explanation: A `template.tsx` is like a layout but it creates a NEW instance on every navigation — it re-mounts, resetting its state and re-running effects. Use a template when you specifically WANT per-navigation behavior (enter/exit animations, per-page analytics on mount, resetting a form). Use a layout (the default) when you want persistence.

subtopics.title: Metadata in layouts and pages
subtopics.explanation: Both `layout.tsx` and `page.tsx` can export a `metadata` object (or a `generateMetadata` function) to set `<title>`, description, and Open Graph tags. Metadata merges down the tree: the root sets defaults, a layout can override for a section, and a page can override for itself. A `title.template` in a parent lets children fill in just their part.

subtopics.title: Special files alongside page and layout
subtopics.explanation: Each segment can also define `loading.tsx` (a Suspense fallback shown while the page loads), `error.tsx` (an error boundary for the segment), and `not-found.tsx`. These compose with layouts so a slow or failing page shows fallback UI without tearing down the surrounding layout.

foundations.overview: The App Router builds UI from the filesystem: folders define URL segments, and two special files give each segment meaning. `page.tsx` is the leaf UI that makes a route reachable; `layout.tsx` is the surrounding UI shared by that route and its descendants. Layouts persist across navigation, which is what makes app-shell patterns (sidebars, nav bars, players) feel instant.
foundations.formalDefinition: A page is the default-exported component of a segment's `page.tsx`, rendered as the unique content for that URL. A layout is the default-exported component of a `layout.tsx` that receives `children` and wraps the segment's page plus all nested segments, sharing one instance across navigations within its subtree.
foundations.whyItMatters: Understanding pages vs layouts is the foundation of App Router structure: it determines what's reachable, what's shared, what persists, and where global concerns (html shell, providers, metadata) live. Most routing bugs and unnecessary re-renders trace back to misunderstanding the page/layout split.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of layouts as nested picture frames and the page as the picture inside the innermost frame. Navigating swaps the picture (page) while the frames (layouts) stay on the wall. The root layout is the wall itself — the html/body document.
foundations.browserPerspective: On first load the browser receives fully-rendered HTML for the whole layout→page tree. On subsequent in-app navigations, Next swaps only the changed page segment's RSC payload into the existing layout, so the browser keeps the persisted layout DOM and its state intact.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A dashboard app uses a root layout for fonts/providers, a `(dashboard)` layout for the sidebar and top bar, and individual pages for Overview, Settings, and Billing — so switching tabs keeps the sidebar mounted and scroll position preserved.
foundations.businessImpact: Persistent layouts make multi-page apps feel like single-page apps, improving perceived speed and engagement, while the file-based structure lets teams onboard quickly because the URL map mirrors the folder tree.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Co-locating routing, UI, loading, and error states by folder reduces wiring and keeps related code together. Shared layouts eliminate duplicated chrome and centralize providers, cutting boilerplate across pages.
foundations.performanceImpact: Because layouts don't re-render on navigation, layout-level data fetches and expensive components aren't repeated per page. Pairing layouts with `loading.tsx` enables streaming and instant navigation feedback.
commonUseCases: Root layout for the html/body shell, fonts, and global providers
Section layouts for sidebars and nav bars that persist across pages
Templates for per-navigation animations or analytics that need a fresh mount
Per-page or per-section metadata for SEO and social previews

commonMisconceptions.myth: A folder is a route as soon as it exists.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A folder is only navigable once it contains a `page.tsx` (or a route handler). Without one, the folder is just structure and returns a 404.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Layouts re-render when you navigate between their child pages.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Layouts persist — they stay mounted and keep their state across navigations within their subtree. Use a `template.tsx` if you actually want a fresh instance per navigation.

steps.name: Navigate

steps.name: Metadata merge
steps.detail: metadata from root, section layout, and page merge top-down to produce the final <head> for the route.

codeLab.title: Build a persistent layout with a children slot
codeLab.instructions: Edit the Layout component so it renders a heading 'My App' and then renders its `children`. The App switches between two pages; confirm the heading stays put while the page content changes. Then Run.
codeLab.expectedOutput: A 'My App' header that stays visible while the page text switches between Home and About.
hints: A layout MUST render its `children` prop, or nested pages won't appear.
Put the shared header above {children}; everything inside {children} is the swappable page.

debuggingLab.title: Layout renders but the page is blank
debuggingLab.symptom: The sidebar/header shows, but the actual page content never appears under it.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: A layout's job is to wrap its page, and Next passes the page UI in as the `children` prop. If the layout never renders `{children}`, the page content has nowhere to appear — you see only the layout chrome. This is the single most common layout bug.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to render `{children}` inside the layout.
Naming the prop something else or not destructuring it, so `children` is undefined.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Render `{children}` inside the layout, below the sidebar, so the page content shows.

theory.question: What is the difference between page.tsx and layout.tsx in the App Router?
theory.directAnswer: A `page.tsx` defines the unique UI for a route segment and is what makes that URL publicly reachable. A `layout.tsx` defines shared UI that wraps a segment's page and all nested segments via a required `children` prop. The crucial difference is lifecycle: pages swap on navigation, while layouts persist (stay mounted, keep state) across navigations within their subtree.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: page.tsx = leaf route UI; layout.tsx = shared wrapper UI that receives children and surrounds the page.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To separate per-route content from shared chrome (nav, sidebars, providers) so the shared parts can persist and not be re-rendered or re-fetched on every navigation.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Next builds a tree from the folder structure: each layout wraps the next layout/page down the path, and only the changing page segment is swapped on client navigation.

theory.whyImportant: It's the foundational App Router concept; understanding the page/layout split is required to reason about routing, persistence, data fetching, and re-renders.
theory.realWorldExample: A dashboard's sidebar lives in a layout so it stays mounted (preserving scroll/state) while Overview, Settings, and Billing pages swap underneath it.

nestedTopics.title: children prop
nestedTopics.explanation: Layouts must render `{children}`, the slot where the nested layout or page is injected.

nestedTopics.title: Persistence
nestedTopics.explanation: Layouts don't unmount on navigation, so layout state and data fetches aren't repeated.

nestedTopics.title: Reachability
nestedTopics.explanation: A folder needs a page.tsx (or route handler) to become a navigable URL.

followUps.question: How do you make a folder NOT reachable as a route?
followUps.answer: Omit its page.tsx — without a page (or route handler) the segment is just structure and returns 404. Route groups `(name)` also organize without affecting the URL.

followUps.question: Can a layout fetch data?
followUps.answer: Yes — a Server Component layout can be async and fetch data; because it persists, that fetch isn't repeated when navigating between its child pages.

theory.question: What is the difference between a layout and a template, and when would you use a template?
theory.directAnswer: Both wrap their children, but a layout persists across navigation (one shared instance that keeps state), while a template creates a NEW instance on every navigation — it re-mounts, resetting state and re-running effects. Use a template when you specifically want per-navigation behavior: enter/exit animations, resetting a form between pages, or running an effect on each route change.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: layout.tsx = persistent wrapper; template.tsx = wrapper that re-mounts per navigation.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The default (layout) optimizes for persistence/perf; templates exist for cases where fresh state per navigation is the desired behavior.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: On navigation Next reuses the layout instance but remounts the template, giving the template's children new DOM and a fresh component lifecycle.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing wrong causes subtle bugs — animations that don't replay, or state that unexpectedly resets — so interviewers probe whether you understand the lifecycle difference.
theory.realWorldExample: A wizard that should restart its step state on each new entry uses a template; a sidebar that should keep its scroll position uses a layout.

nestedTopics.title: Re-mount semantics
nestedTopics.explanation: A template's effects re-run and its useState resets on every navigation.

nestedTopics.title: Composition
nestedTopics.explanation: If both exist in a segment, the template renders inside the layout, around the children.

followUps.question: Where does a template sit relative to a layout?
followUps.answer: Inside it: the layout wraps the template, which wraps the page's children. So the layout persists while the template inside it re-mounts.

scenario.question: Your app has a sidebar that re-fetches its data and loses scroll position every time the user navigates between dashboard pages. What's likely wrong and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The sidebar is probably rendered inside each page (or inside a template), so it re-mounts on every navigation. Move it into a shared `layout.tsx` for the dashboard segment. Because layouts persist across navigations within their subtree, the sidebar will stay mounted — keeping its scroll position and avoiding the repeated data fetch.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A persistence problem caused by putting shared chrome in the wrong place.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Shared UI placed at the page level (or in a template) re-mounts per navigation instead of persisting.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A `layout.tsx` at app/dashboard/ wraps every dashboard page; Next keeps that one instance mounted while only the page swaps.

scenario.whyImportant: Placement of shared UI is a daily App Router decision that directly affects perceived performance and correctness.

nestedTopics.title: Layout data fetch
nestedTopics.explanation: Fetch the sidebar's data in the layout so it runs once and isn't repeated per page.

nestedTopics.title: Template caveat
nestedTopics.explanation: If the sidebar must persist, ensure it isn't inside a template, which would re-mount it.

followUps.question: What if only one page should NOT show the sidebar?
followUps.answer: Use route groups to give that page a different layout, e.g. put it in a separate group without the sidebar layout.

coding.question: Write a root layout and a nested dashboard layout for the App Router, including a metadata title template.
coding.thoughtProcess: The root layout must render <html>/<body> and is the place for global metadata; I'll add a title.template so child pages fill in their own title. The dashboard layout adds a persistent sidebar and renders children. Both must accept and render the children prop.
coding.lineByLine: The root layout sets a metadata title template ('%s | Acme') and renders the document shell with {children}. The dashboard layout adds a persistent sidebar and renders {children} in <main>. The settings page exports its own metadata title, which the template turns into 'Settings | Acme'. Every layout renders {children}, so the tree composes correctly.

alternativeApproaches.title: Dynamic metadata
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use generateMetadata when the title depends on fetched data.

followUps.question: Why can only the root layout render <html> and <body>?
followUps.answer: The root layout replaces the document shell for the whole app; nested layouts render inside that body, so they only render fragments/elements, not another html/body.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Model the app as a tree of layouts with pages at the leaves. Put global concerns (html/body, fonts, providers, error/analytics boundaries) in the root layout; put section chrome (nav, sidebars) in section layouts; keep pages focused on unique content. Use route groups `(name)` to share or vary layouts without changing URLs, and reserve templates for the rare cases that need a fresh mount per navigation.
productionDeepDive.performance: Lean on layout persistence: fetch layout-level data once in an async layout so it isn't repeated per page, and pair pages with `loading.tsx` to stream and give instant navigation feedback. Avoid pushing 'use client' up to a layout/page just for a small widget — extract the interactive bit so the rest stays a Server Component.
productionDeepDive.security: Keep auth/session reads and data access in server-side layouts/pages, not leaked to client components. Don't render sensitive data in a layout that persists across routes the user may not be authorized for; gate per-segment instead and validate on the server.
productionDeepDive.scaling: File-based structure scales with team size because the URL map mirrors folders; route groups keep large apps organized. Static layouts/pages serve from the CDN, and per-segment loading/error boundaries isolate failures so one slow page doesn't break the whole shell.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Co-locating page, layout, loading, and error files per segment keeps related code together and makes ownership obvious. A single root layout centralizes providers and metadata defaults, reducing duplication and drift across pages.
productionDeepDive.observability: Per-segment error.tsx boundaries surface failures with context, and templates (or layout effects) can log per-navigation analytics. Metadata and the build output's route map make it easy to audit which routes exist and how they're rendered.

caseStudies.problem: Shared navigation re-mounted on every page change, losing state and re-fetching.
caseStudies.solution: Move shared chrome into a section layout that persists; fetch its data in the layout.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Shared state in a persistent layout must be reset deliberately when needed (e.g. via a template for specific subtrees).
caseStudies.lessons: Place shared UI at the right layout level; default to layouts and reach for templates only when fresh mounts are required.

keyTakeaways: A folder becomes a reachable route only when it has a page.tsx; that default export is the route's unique UI.
A layout.tsx wraps its page and all nested segments via a required {children} prop and persists across navigation (state and data survive).
Exactly one root layout (app/layout.tsx) is required and is the only layout that renders <html> and <body>.
Layouts nest by folder depth; a template.tsx is like a layout but re-mounts on every navigation for fresh state/animations.
Both layouts and pages can export metadata, which merges top-down — use a title.template in a parent and override per page.
